section_summary: This section closes with a Spanish-language defense of the Japanese immigrant community’s contributions to Peru, followed by U.S. diplomatic records assessing alleged Japanese political, commercial, intelligence, and propaganda activity. Embassy officers largely discredit Héctor de Paulet Wilquet’s allegations but document increasingly assertive Japanese cultivation of Peruvian officials, economic interests, cultural missions, and public opinion. The final pages contain filing and cross-reference sheets on espionage suspicions and the perceived Japanese threat, a despatch reporting Prefect Meave’s views, and an earlier memorandum about Japanese propaganda in Chile.

subfiles.title: Japanese Immigrants and Their Contributions to Peru — Conclusion
subfiles.about: The article defends the economic, agricultural, and social contributions of Japanese immigrants in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Kurotobi supplies population figures for Japanese communities in numerous Peruvian towns and describes their work in agriculture, fishing, cafés, barber shops, bakeries, bazaars, and other small industries. He emphasizes their honesty, labor, employment of Peruvians, compliance with regulations, and attachment to Peru as a second homeland. The conclusion offers wishes for Peru’s continued peace and prosperity on behalf of the Japanese Central Society of Peru.

subfiles.title: Document File Note on Héctor de Paulet Wilquet’s Allegations
subfiles.about: The note indexes allegations that Japanese financing of a Peruvian Fascist group could cause a change of government within sixty days.
subfiles.summary: The filing note identifies information supplied by former Peruvian vice consul Héctor de Paulet Wilquet. It records his claim that a Peruvian Fascist group had received considerable financial assistance from the Japanese government and that a change of government was imminent.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 382: Inquiry of the Federal Bureau of Investigation Regarding Japanese Activities in Peru
subfiles.from: Laurence A. Steinhardt, American Embassy in Lima
subfiles.about: Steinhardt evaluates and largely rejects information supplied to the FBI by Héctor de Paulet Wilquet about Japanese activities in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Steinhardt reports that Peru had made no guano sales or shipments to Japanese interests since 1932 and finds no evidence of imminent political upheaval or Japanese financing of a Peruvian group. He argues that Peru’s guarded ports, coast, roads, and government-controlled guano operations would make substantial clandestine arms or guano shipments difficult. He also questions Wilquet’s credibility because of his reputation and family estrangement, while acknowledging reported visa or passport corruption at the Peruvian consulate in Hong Kong. Any arms-for-guano dealings, he concludes, would probably have occurred before 1932.

subfiles.title: Department Instruction Requesting Comments on FBI Information
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department forwards an FBI communication on Japanese activities in Peru and asks Ambassador Steinhardt for comments.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses the March 11 communication from the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. That communication transmitted information gathered by the Bureau’s Honolulu office concerning alleged Japanese activities in Peru.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Document File Note on Wilquet’s Allegations
subfiles.about: This duplicate filing note cross-references the Justice Department letter containing Wilquet’s allegations about Japanese support for Peruvian Fascists.
subfiles.summary: The note repeats the allegation that a change of government in Peru could occur within sixty days. It attributes the prediction to former vice consul Héctor de Paulet Wilquet and to alleged Japanese financial aid for a Fascist group.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 679: Effectiveness of Japanese Propaganda
subfiles.from: Louis G. Dreyfus Jr., American Embassy in Lima
subfiles.about: Dreyfus describes aggressive Japanese social diplomacy toward Manuel B. Llosa and growing Peruvian resentment of Japanese propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The new Japanese minister pressed Manuel B. Llosa to accept a farewell cocktail party before Llosa departed for the New York and San Francisco world fairs. Dreyfus interprets the presence of Foreign Office and Fomento officials as an attempt to cultivate agencies responsible for concessions. He reports that Japanese publicity surrounding a recent Peruvian cultural mission to Japan had bred suspicion, causing even invitations and social gestures to be viewed with distrust. In his judgment, Japanese excessive zeal was defeating its own purposes.

subfiles.title: Document File Note on Japanese–Peruvian Relations
subfiles.from: Louis G. Dreyfus Jr., American Embassy in Peru
subfiles.about: The note summarizes Japan’s attempts to cultivate Peruvian favor and the unfriendly response among officials and workers.
subfiles.summary: The filing note refers to the warm Japanese reception of the Peruvian Cultural and Economic Mission and to the Japanese minister’s activities in Peru. It nevertheless characterizes opinion toward Japan as decidedly unfriendly in both high official circles and the proletariat.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 668: Japanese–Peruvian Economic Relations
subfiles.from: Louis G. Dreyfus Jr., American Embassy in Lima
subfiles.about: Dreyfus reports on Japanese publicity and commercial overtures associated with the Peruvian Cultural and Economic Mission in Japan.
subfiles.summary: United Press reports emphasized expanded trade and friendship, but the Peruvian Foreign Office and National Industrial Society insisted that the visiting mission was unofficial and lacked authority to negotiate commercial agreements. The Japanese minister offered to arrange a purchase of approximately 50,000 bales of lower-grade Peruvian cotton, though the proposed price was unacceptable. Dreyfus views the mission’s reception and the minister’s activity as a coordinated effort to gain favor, while noting strong anti-Japanese feeling in official and working-class circles. He found no recent evidence of joint Japanese–Peruvian exploitation of mineral, petroleum, or fishing resources.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Note on Totalitarian Propaganda and the Peruvian Mission to Japan
subfiles.from: Laurence A. Steinhardt, American Embassy in Peru
subfiles.about: The note directs readers to a memorandum discussing Japanese propaganda about the Peruvian economic and cultural mission.
subfiles.summary: Japanese-inspired rumors repeatedly claimed that the mission had negotiated commercial and other agreements with Japan. The Peruvian Foreign Office was repeatedly obliged to deny these reports, causing considerable annoyance and vexation.

subfiles.title: Document File Note on Japanese Activities During the Pan-American Conference
subfiles.from: Laurence A. Steinhardt, American Embassy in Peru
subfiles.about: The note indexes a despatch about Japanese charitable and cultural publicity during the Pan-American Conference.
subfiles.summary: The referenced despatch enclosed an El Comercio clipping about a gift from the Japanese Central Society to Lima Public Charities. It also enclosed an El Universal article about a society reception presenting a Japanese dancer.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 806: Japanese Activities During the Eighth Inter-American Conference
subfiles.from: Laurence A. Steinhardt, American Embassy in Lima
subfiles.about: Steinhardt reports that Japanese organizations continued public-relations efforts while the inter-American conference met in Lima.
subfiles.summary: The despatch forwards material about a Japanese-colony donation to Lima Public Charities. It also reports a Japanese Central Society reception for dancer Suzuko Takano, attended by professors, intellectuals, art patrons, society figures, and members of the recently returned Peruvian mission to Japan. Steinhardt presents both events as efforts to win Peruvian public favor.

subfiles.title: Exchange of Letters Concerning the Japanese Central Society’s Charitable Donation
subfiles.doc_type: translated newspaper clipping and despatch enclosure
subfiles.from: Japanese Central Society of Peru and Lima Public Charities
subfiles.about: The translated correspondence records a Japanese Central Society donation to Lima Public Charities and the charity’s acknowledgment.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese Central Society describes its contribution as support for the humanitarian work performed by Lima Public Charities. The recipient formally acknowledges the enclosed cheque and expresses thanks for the donation.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: “Japanese Menace Seen by a Peruvian”
subfiles.about: The note indexes Farley’s letter enclosing a clipping about working conditions in Peru and a perceived Japanese menace.
subfiles.summary: The filing note gives the clipping’s title as “Japanese Menace Seen by a Peruvian.” It characterizes the enclosed material as concerning working conditions in Peru.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Note: Review of Peligro América
subfiles.from: Louis G. Dreyfus Jr., American Embassy in Peru
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references a review of a Peruvian book advocating closer hemispheric cooperation against a Japanese threat.
subfiles.summary: The reviewed book, Peligro América, urges Peru and other countries of the Americas to establish closer political, economic, and military ties with the United States. Its author presents Japan as a threat to the continent. The original item was filed as Despatch No. 1088.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Note on Fanji Uchida
subfiles.from: Louis G. Dreyfus Jr., American Embassy in Peru
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report on Fanji Uchida’s suspicious conduct aboard a Panagra flight from Guayaquil to Lima.
subfiles.summary: The referenced report followed the movements of Japanese national Fanji Uchida on a Panagra aircraft. The filing officer judged those movements to have the earmarks of espionage. The original was Despatch No. 1108.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Note on Prefect Meave’s Warning About Japanese Activities
subfiles.from: Louis G. Dreyfus Jr., American Embassy in Peru
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to Prefect Meave’s statement about Japanese activities in Latin America and his warning that Japanese nationals required constant observation.
subfiles.summary: The filing note identifies Señor Meave as Prefect of Lima. It summarizes his concern about Japanese activities across Latin America and his recommendation that the Japanese be watched continually. The original was Despatch No. 1511.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1511: Interview with Prefect Meave
subfiles.from: Louis G. Dreyfus Jr., American Embassy in Lima
subfiles.about: The despatch records Prefect Meave’s views on Japanese activities, personal grievances, and Peruvian political conditions.
subfiles.summary: The surviving, internally misordered pages contain Meave’s comments about Japanese nationals and his broader assessment of Peruvian politics. He discusses the Benavides administration, APRA, Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre, and the Miró Quesada faction, stating that neither Haya nor APRA was then gaining strength. Meave praises Minister of Gobierno Guillermo Garrido Lecca as honest and gentlemanly while condemning former ministers Antonio Rodríguez and Diómedes Arias Schreiber.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese Propaganda in Chile
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes a Santiago despatch reporting Japanese propaganda in Chile concerning Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese legation in Chile was reportedly distributing pro-Japanese material about the Manchurian situation. Radio was apparently also being used, including a University of Concepción professor’s talk that strongly favored the Japanese viewpoint. The information came from Santiago’s Despatch No. 1337 of December 20, 1932.
